_readme: Single source of truth for every legal, contact and pricing fact on the site. Anything marked FILL_ME must be filled in before the site will build. See build.js. Change a value here and every page that mentions it updates on the next build.

databases.note: Pick whichever your project needs. It runs on the same machine as your application, so a query is a loopback call and never crosses the internet.

vector.short: Vector search is included. PostgreSQL ships with pgvector switched on.
vector.why: A separate vector database would want its own memory and its own bill. pgvector is an extension rather than another service, so your embeddings sit in the same database as the rest of your data and cost nothing extra.

limits.imagesText: the build you are running and the one before it
limits.storageNote: The storage allowance is a ceiling, not a reservation, and it covers everything the application owns: your code, the files it writes, your uploads and your database, counted together.
limits.persistentNote: Anything your application writes to /data stays there through a deploy. Files it writes anywhere else are part of the container and go when you next push.

runtimes.note: We read your repository and work out how to build it. If your language is not on that list, or you want the build done your way, add a Dockerfile and we build that instead. Rust, Elixir, Deno, Bun, C++, anything that starts and listens on a port.

company.operatedBy: This website is operated by Rohit Mahto, a sole proprietor trading as DormHost.

gst.statement: DormHost is not registered for GST. The price you see is the full amount charged. No tax is added at checkout.

refund.mode: the original payment method, meaning the same UPI ID, card or bank account you paid from
refund.short: We refund credit you have not spent. Days your application was actually hosted are not refunded, because the price does not carry a free trial period twice.
refund.faultOfOurs: Neither of the two limits applies when the fault is ours.

policies.retentionNote: If your balance runs out we keep everything for 30 days, or 7 days if you have never added credit of your own. We email you before anything is deleted, and adding credit at any point stops it.

payments.methods: UPI, debit card, credit card and net banking
payments.methodsIntl: Visa, Mastercard and American Express, charged in Indian Rupees
payments.currencyNote: Everything is priced and charged in Indian Rupees (INR, ₹), wherever you are. An international card works: your bank converts the rupee amount at its own rate and may add a foreign transaction fee, so the figure on your statement will be close to, but not exactly, the dollar approximation shown here.

annual.note: Pay for ten months, get twelve. Adding a year of credit in one go changes what you are charged each day for that plan, for 365 days.
annual.whatItIs: It changes your daily rate, not your term. Your balance still goes down every day, so running two applications on the plan uses a year of credit in about half a year. Whatever is left is yours, and refundable under the refund policy.
annual.perDay: Nap works out at about ₹3.30 a day paying monthly, or about ₹2.74 a day if you add a year at once. Awake is about ₹8.30 a day monthly, or about ₹6.85 a day for the year. We take the day's share out of your balance each morning, and a full month or a full year always adds up to exactly the price on this page.

wallet.howItWorks: You add money to a balance and we take each day's share of your plan out of it. Nothing renews on its own and no card is stored.
wallet.firstDay: Creating an application charges its first day straight away, so you need enough in your balance to cover that day before you can create one.
wallet.whenItRuns: The day's charge is taken once each day, on UTC. A full month of daily charges comes to exactly the monthly price, and a full year comes to exactly the yearly price.
wallet.empty: If your balance reaches zero your application is stopped, not deleted. Add credit and it starts again with everything as you left it. We keep your data for 30 days after that.
wallet.leftover: Whatever is left in your balance is yours. We refund it on request under the refund policy, or you can leave it on the account for later, where it does not expire.

ai.pitch: Pay for AI in rupees from the balance you already have. No card, no minimum, and it works with any OpenAI SDK.
ai.injected: Apps hosted on DormHost get OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY set automatically, so AI works from inside your app with zero configuration. Set either variable yourself, to use OpenAI directly for example, and your value wins.
ai.billing: Billed per request from the provider's reported cost at our daily exchange rate. Prices can change daily and without notice, whenever provider list prices or the exchange rate move. Trial credit does not cover AI; it needs paid balance.
ai.example: A short chat on the cheapest model costs well under a rupee, and an image is a few rupees.

trial.headline: Seven days free, no credit card required
trial.short: Sign in with GitHub and we put seven days of Nap credit in your balance.
trial.what: Signing in with GitHub for the first time puts seven days of Nap credit in your balance. It is real credit and it is spent the same way as any other: a day at a time, so you can see exactly what your app costs while you try it.
trial.limits: Free credit runs one application on the Nap plan. Adding any credit of your own lifts that, and you can then run as many applications as your balance covers, on either plan.
trial.after: When the free credit runs out your application is stopped, not deleted. Add credit and it comes back exactly as it was. One free trial per GitHub account.
trial.noCard: We do not ask for a credit card and there is nothing to cancel.

howto._readme: The dashboard procedure, written once. Every step names a control that exists in the dashboard today. If the dashboard changes, change it here and every page follows.

quickstart.title: Sign in with GitHub
quickstart.text: Go to the dashboard and sign in. Your first sign-in puts seven days of Nap credit in your balance, with no card and nothing to cancel.

quickstart.title: Create an application
quickstart.text: Press New app and give it a name: three characters or more, letters, numbers and hyphens. The address is shown under the field as you type, and it is yourapp-yourlogin.dormhost.app.

quickstart.title: Pick the plan
quickstart.text: Nap sleeps when nobody is using it. Awake never sleeps, which is what a bot, a worker or a scheduled job needs. Awake also lets you choose Mumbai, London or Ashburn; Nap goes wherever there is room.

quickstart.title: Point it at your repository
quickstart.text: Paste the GitHub URL and the branch. Press Connect GitHub to pick from a list instead, which is also how a private repository is deployed. Then press Create and deploy.

quickstart.title: Watch the build log
quickstart.text: The application opens on Overview, and Live logs streams the build. Listen on the port in the PORT variable we set, or EXPOSE one port in your Dockerfile, and the address answers as soon as the build finishes.

next.title: Add a database
next.text: Open the Database section, choose PostgreSQL with pgvector, MongoDB or MariaDB, and press Add a database. The connection string arrives in your app as DATABASE_URL, or MONGODB_URI on MongoDB, so there is nothing to copy.

next.title: Set environment variables
next.text: The Environment section takes both variables and whole files, for a service-account JSON or a certificate. Saving restarts the app, which takes a few seconds.

next.title: Deploy on every push
next.text: The Deploy card on Overview has a Deploy on push switch. Turn it on, then copy the payload URL and secret it shows into your repository on GitHub, under Settings, Webhooks, Add webhook. Content type application/json, and only the push event.

next.title: Point your own domain at it
next.text: In Domains, add the name, then add your domain to your own Cloudflare, add a CNAME to your dormhost.app address, and press Check. Your app answers on both addresses.

next.title: Or run WordPress instead
next.text: Choose WordPress on the create form and there is no repository at all. We run it, create its MariaDB, finish the install and show you the admin password on the app page, where you can also reset it.

next.title: Roll back, and take a backup
next.text: Images keeps the build you are running and the one before it, so a bad deploy is one click from the working one. Backups takes one on demand, and Awake also takes one every night.

Open the address and WordPress asks you for a title and an admin user, which is its own five minute install and the only setup there is.
bullets: No repository and no build; the site exists as soon as it is created
MariaDB is created with the app, so there is no connection string to copy
Plugins, themes and uploads are kept, and survive a restart
WordPress updates its own core, in place
An HTTPS address immediately, or a custom domain through your own Cloudflare
Backups cover the whole site: the files and the database together
steps: Sign in to the dashboard and press New app.
Choose WordPress under "What are you deploying?". The repository fields disappear, because there is no repository.
Name it and pick a plan. Nap sleeps when nobody is visiting, which makes the first visit after that take a few seconds. Awake stays up.
Press Create my site, then open your address. WordPress asks for a site title and an admin user.
Install an SMTP plugin before you rely on password resets. Mail does not leave the container, so WordPress cannot send you a reset link on its own.
Take a backup from the Backups section before you install anything risky. It captures the files and the database in one archive.

steps: Make Express listen on the port we set: app.listen(process.env.PORT || 3000). That is the one line most MERN projects have to change.
Build React into the folder Express serves, from the build script in the root package.json, so one deploy ships the API and the frontend together.
Add MongoDB in the Database section. It arrives in the app as MONGODB_URI, so read that rather than a hard-coded localhost string.
Put your JWT secret and any API keys in the Environment section. They are set at start and never sit in the repository.

faq.q: What can I host on DormHost?
faq.a: Any web application in any language. Node.js, Python, Go, Java, Ruby, PHP and .NET are detected and built automatically, anything else builds from a Dockerfile, and bots or workers run on Awake, which never sleeps.

faq.q: Do I need a database elsewhere?
faq.a: No. MongoDB, PostgreSQL or MariaDB run on the same machine as your application, so queries are loopback calls, and PostgreSQL includes pgvector for embeddings.

faq.q: How do I deploy every time I push?
faq.a: Turn on Deploy on push from the Deploy card on your application's Overview, then add the payload URL and secret it gives you as a webhook on GitHub. Until that hook exists, deploys happen when you ask for them.

blogPosts.title: How to deploy a MERN project online
blogPosts.meta: Deploy a MERN stack project online: connect your GitHub repo, add your MongoDB connection string, and get a live URL in minutes.
blogPosts.lede: A MERN project is four moving parts, but only two need hosting: the Node.js server and the database. React is built and served by that same server. So a MERN deploy is really a Node.js deploy plus a MongoDB connection string.
body: The React build is served by the Express process, so the frontend and the API are one deploy rather than two, and there is no CORS to configure.
steps: Change one line before you start: app.listen(process.env.PORT || 3000). A hard-coded port builds cleanly and then answers nothing.
Make the root build script build React into the folder Express serves, so npm run build produces the whole application.
Sign in to the dashboard with GitHub, press New app, and name it. The address under the field is the one you will share.
Choose Nap, paste the repository URL and branch, and press Create and deploy. Press Connect GitHub first if the repository is private.
Open Database, choose MongoDB, and press Add a database. It appears in the app as MONGODB_URI, so read that instead of a localhost string.
Open Environment and add your JWT secret and any API keys. Saving restarts the app with them.
Watch Live logs until the build finishes, then open the address. Turn on Deploy on push from the Deploy card, add the webhook it shows you on GitHub, and the next commit deploys itself.
blogPosts.cta: Deploy your MERN project for free

blogPosts.title: How to host a Python project online (Flask or FastAPI)
blogPosts.meta: Host a Flask or FastAPI project online: install from requirements.txt, run the app, and add a database on the same machine.
blogPosts.lede: Python web projects are mostly Flask or FastAPI, and both go online the same way: install the dependencies and run the app. The database is the part students usually get stuck on, which is why DormHost puts one on the same machine.
body: Flask and FastAPI deploy the same way. The only difference is the command that starts the server, and both have to bind the port the platform hands them rather than a port they choose.
steps: Commit requirements.txt or pyproject.toml. The build installs from it, so anything missing there is missing in production.
Bind to 0.0.0.0 and the PORT variable: uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT for FastAPI, gunicorn app:app --bind 0.0.0.0:$PORT for Flask.
Sign in to the dashboard with GitHub, press New app, name it, and pick Nap. Awake is for bots, scrapers and scheduled work.
Paste the repository URL and branch, then press Create and deploy. Live logs shows the pip install and the start command as they run.
Open Database, choose PostgreSQL, and press Add a database. It arrives as DATABASE_URL with pgvector already enabled, which is what an embeddings project needs.
Open Environment for your API keys and read them with os.environ. Saving restarts the app.
If the app crashes at start, the traceback is in Live logs. It is almost always a missing dependency or a port that was not read from PORT.
blogPosts.cta: Deploy your Python project for free

blogPosts.title: How to deploy your final year project online
blogPosts.meta: Get your final year project online for the viva: a live URL, a real database and hosting priced in rupees from ₹99 a month.
blogPosts.lede: A final year project deserves a live demo, not a laptop passed around the room. A URL is also something concrete to put in the report and on the resume. Here is how to get one without a credit card or a server of your own.
body: Hosting is ₹99 a month on Nap, charged in rupees by UPI or card, and unused credit is refundable under the refund policy. A semester of it costs less than the printing bill for the report.
steps: Sign in to the dashboard with GitHub. The first sign-in puts seven days of credit in your balance, with no card, which is enough to rehearse the demo.
Push the project to GitHub. Node.js, Python, Go, Java, Ruby, PHP and .NET are detected automatically; anything else needs a Dockerfile in the repository root.
Press New app, name it, choose Nap, and paste the repository URL and branch. The address shown under the name field is what goes in your report.
Press Create and deploy, then watch Live logs. Your app has to listen on the port in the PORT variable, which is the usual reason a first deploy answers nothing.
Open Database, pick the engine your project uses, and press Add a database. The connection string is set in the app already, as DATABASE_URL or MONGODB_URI.
Move every credential out of settings files and into the Environment section before you submit the code.
The night before the viva, take a backup from the Backups section and check that the previous build is still in Images, so a late change can be undone in one click.
Open the app a few minutes before you present. A Nap app sleeps after fifteen minutes idle, and this way the panel gets it already awake.
blogPosts.cta: Deploy your final year project for free
